name: Cancún · Isla Mujeres
tagline: Caribbean beaches and the gateway to the Yucatán
summary: Mexico's busiest resort: a 22 km strip of hotels on white sand, a real Mexican downtown, and the ferry to laid-back Isla Mujeres. Most visitors use it as the arrival point for Tulum, the cenotes and Chichén Itzá.
seasonNote: Hurricane season runs June to November, peaking in September and October; sargassum seaweed can cover beaches from May to August; spring break in March is loud and busy.
arrival: Cancún airport is 20 minutes from the Hotel Zone; ADO buses run to downtown, Playa del Carmen and Tulum.
gettingAround: R1 and R2 buses run the length of the Hotel Zone day and night; ferries to Isla Mujeres leave from Puerto Juárez and the Hotel Zone.
cashTip: Pay in pesos, not dollars, to avoid poor exchange rates; use bank ATMs inside shops or malls.
foodTip: Eat downtown for tacos al pastor, cochinita pibil and fresh ceviche at local prices.
buyTip: Hammocks, vanilla and huipil embroidery at Mercado 28.
baseArea: The Hotel Zone for the beach; downtown for prices and food; Isla Mujeres for calm

connections.note: ADO buses from the airport and downtown; the Tren Maya also runs.
ADO buses; the Tren Maya also runs.

items.name: Playa Delfines
items.summary: A wide public beach with turquoise water and the Cancún sign above it.
items.expect: Strong waves and red-flag days; few facilities.
items.tip: Come early for the colour of the water and bring shade.
items.why: The best free beach in Cancún.
flow: Photo at the sign, then the beach.

items.name: Isla Mujeres
items.summary: A small island of calm shallow water, golf carts and seafood, 20 minutes by ferry.
items.expect: Playa Norte is busy at midday.
items.tip: Rent a golf cart to the cliffs at Punta Sur, then swim at Playa Norte for sunset.
items.why: The Caribbean as it was before the resorts.
flow: Golf cart round the island, then Playa Norte.

items.name: MUSA underwater museum
items.summary: Hundreds of sculptures on the sea floor, now covered in coral, seen by snorkel, dive or glass-bottom boat.
items.expect: Visibility depends on weather; tours include a reef stop.
items.tip: Snorkelling suits the shallow Manchones site; divers see more.
items.why: An art installation that became a reef.
flow: Boat from the Hotel Zone or Isla Mujeres.

items.name: Museo Maya de Cancún and San Miguelito
items.summary: A modern museum of Maya finds with a small ruined Maya site in the jungle behind it.
items.expect: Closed on Mondays; quiet.
items.tip: Good on a rainy or sargassum day.
items.why: The best introduction to the Maya before seeing the big sites.
flow: Museum halls, then the trail to San Miguelito.

items.name: Chichén Itzá
items.summary: The great Maya-Toltec city with the stepped pyramid of El Castillo, one of the New Seven Wonders.
items.expect: Two and a half hours each way; vendors and heat inside; arrive at 8 am to beat the tours.
items.tip: Better visited from Mérida or Valladolid; add Cenote Ik Kil on the way.
items.why: The most famous Maya site.
flow: El Castillo, the ball court, then the sacred cenote.

items.name: Mercado 28 and downtown
items.summary: The local side of Cancún: a market of crafts and canteens and the evening square of Parque de las Palapas.
items.expect: Touts at the market; families in the park at night.
items.tip: Go in the evening for the food stalls in Parque de las Palapas.
items.why: Where Cancún residents eat and shop.
flow: R1 or R2 bus to downtown.
Mercado 28, then Parque de las Palapas.

items.name: Taquería El Polilla
items.summary: A family taquería serving Yucatecan pork tacos and tortas in the mornings.
items.expect: Closes in the early afternoon.
items.tip: Order cochinita pibil and lechón with pickled onion.
items.why: Local breakfast at local prices.

items.name: El Fish Fritanga
items.summary: A casual seafood spot on the lagoon side of the Hotel Zone with sand under the tables.
items.expect: Relaxed and popular at sunset.
items.tip: Sit at the water's edge for sunset over the lagoon.
items.why: Good fish at fair prices in the Hotel Zone.

items.name: Parque de las Palapas food stalls
items.summary: Evening stalls around the downtown square selling marquesitas, esquites and tacos.
items.expect: Busiest at weekends.
items.tip: Try a marquesita, a rolled crêpe with Edam cheese.
items.why: The cheapest snacks in town.

name: Tulum · Riviera Maya
tagline: Maya ruins on a cliff, cenotes and jungle beaches
summary: A Maya walled city above the sea, a strip of boutique beach hotels and the region's best cenotes. Playa del Carmen, Cozumel and the Coba ruins are all within an hour.
seasonNote: Hurricane season runs June to November; sargassum seaweed can arrive from May to August.
arrival: Tulum's new airport is 25 minutes away; Cancún airport is two hours by ADO bus. The Tren Maya stops here.
gettingAround: Rent a bicycle between town and the beach; colectivo vans run along Highway 307 to the cenotes and Playa del Carmen.
cashTip: Carry pesos for cenote entry, colectivos and taco stands; beach clubs take cards.
foodTip: Tacos in town, seafood on the beach road and fresh juices everywhere.
buyTip: Hammocks, Mexican textiles and boutique beachwear.
baseArea: Tulum town (Pueblo) for prices; the beach road for the setting

connections.note: ADO buses and the Tren Maya.
ADO buses via Valladolid; the Tren Maya also runs.

items.name: Tulum archaeological site
items.summary: A walled Maya port with the Castillo temple on a cliff above a turquoise cove.
items.expect: Small, very hot and busy from 10 am; no climbing the buildings.
items.tip: Be at the gate at 8 am and bring a swimsuit for the beach below.
items.why: The most beautiful setting of any Maya site.
flow: Walk the loop, then swim at the beach under the Castillo.

items.name: Gran Cenote
items.summary: A clear freshwater sinkhole with caverns, turtles and boardwalks.
items.expect: Shower first and no sunscreen; it is busy by 11 am.
items.tip: Bike from town and arrive at opening; bring snorkel gear.
items.why: The easiest beautiful cenote to reach from Tulum.
flow: Snorkel through the cavern to the second pool.

items.name: Dos Ojos cenotes
items.summary: Two linked cenotes opening into one of the world's longest underwater cave systems.
items.expect: Snorkel tours with lights; cave diving for certified divers.
items.tip: Take a guided snorkel to see the bat cave.
items.why: The most dramatic cave cenote on the coast.
flow: Colectivo towards Playa del Carmen, then a 3 km road.

items.name: Cobá
items.summary: A jungle Maya city of long white roads and the 42-metre Nohoch Mul pyramid.
items.expect: Sites are spread out; rent a bicycle or a pedicab. Climbing the pyramid is no longer allowed.
items.tip: Pair with a swim in the nearby Choo-Ha or Tamcach-Ha cenotes.
items.why: A Maya city still half swallowed by forest.
flow: Bike the sacbé roads to Nohoch Mul.

items.name: Sian Ka'an Biosphere Reserve
items.summary: A UNESCO reserve of lagoons, mangroves and reef south of Tulum, with dolphins and floating channels.
items.expect: A bumpy road; go with a licensed local cooperative.
items.tip: The Muyil route lets you float down an ancient Maya canal.
items.why: The wildest stretch of the Caribbean coast.
flow: Boat through lagoons, float in the canal.

items.name: Akumal turtle bay
items.summary: A shallow bay where green sea turtles graze on sea grass.
items.expect: Life jackets and roped areas; guides are required in part of the bay.
items.tip: Go early and keep your distance from the turtles.
items.why: Almost certain turtle sightings from the beach.

items.name: Cozumel
items.summary: An island famous for world-class drift diving and snorkelling along its reefs.
items.expect: Ferry from Playa del Carmen, 45 minutes; cruise ships fill the town by day.
items.tip: Book a boat to the Palancar or Colombia reefs.
items.why: Some of the best reef diving in the Caribbean.
flow: Colectivo to Playa del Carmen, then the ferry.

items.name: Taquería Honorio
items.summary: A busy taco stand famous for Yucatecan slow-cooked pork.
items.expect: Open from breakfast to early afternoon; it sells out.
items.tip: Order cochinita and relleno negro tacos.
items.why: The best-loved cheap meal in Tulum.

items.name: Hartwood
items.summary: An open-air restaurant cooking everything over wood fire, which helped put Tulum on the food map.
items.expect: Dinner only, a daily-changing menu and high prices.
items.tip: Reservations open a month ahead; walk-in seats exist at opening.
items.why: Tulum's most famous restaurant.
flow: Share several dishes from the fire.

items.name: Antojitos La Chiapaneca
items.summary: A no-frills evening stand with tacos al pastor at very low prices.
items.expect: Plastic stools and a queue.
items.tip: Order al pastor and add pineapple.
items.why: The best value dinner in Tulum.

name: Mérida · Yucatán
tagline: Colonial capital of the Yucatán, cenotes and Maya cities
summary: A safe, colourful colonial city with free culture every evening and the region's best food. It is the base for Uxmal, Chichén Itzá, the cenotes of Cuzamá and the flamingos of Celestún.
seasonNote: April and May are extremely hot, near 40°C; the rainy season from June to October brings afternoon storms.
arrival: Mérida airport is 20 minutes away by taxi; ADO buses link Cancún (4 hours) and Valladolid. The Tren Maya stops here.
gettingAround: Walk the centre; ride-hailing apps are cheap; buses and tours reach the ruins and cenotes.
cashTip: Pesos for markets, colectivos and cenotes.
foodTip: Cochinita pibil, sopa de lima, panuchos, salbutes, papadzules and marquesitas: the Yucatán has its own cuisine.
buyTip: Panama hats, hammocks and guayabera shirts.
baseArea: The Centro Histórico, near Plaza Grande or Paseo de Montejo

connections.note: ADO buses; the Tren Maya also runs.

items.name: Plaza Grande and the Centro Histórico
items.summary: The main square with a 16th-century cathedral, the governor's palace murals and the Casa de Montejo.
items.expect: Busy and lively in the evening, especially at weekends.
items.tip: See the free murals in the Palacio de Gobierno and stay for the evening events.
items.why: The heart of the oldest continuously inhabited city in the Americas' mainland.
flow: Casa de Montejo, then Calle 60 to Parque Santa Lucía.

items.name: Paseo de Montejo
items.summary: A boulevard of French-style mansions built by henequen fibre barons.
items.expect: On Sunday mornings it closes to cars for cycling.
items.tip: Visit the Palacio Cantón museum and the Casa Montejo mansions.
items.why: The wealth of the Yucatán's golden age.
flow: Mansions, then the Monumento a la Patria.

items.name: Gran Museo del Mundo Maya
items.summary: A large modern museum of Maya history, culture and the present-day Maya people.
items.expect: Closed on Tuesdays.
items.tip: Stay for the evening light show on the building.
items.why: The best overview of Maya civilisation in Mexico.

items.name: Uxmal
items.summary: A Maya city with the oval Pyramid of the Magician and finely carved Puuc-style palaces.
items.expect: An hour and a quarter by road; far fewer crowds than Chichén Itzá.
items.tip: Combine with Kabah and the other Puuc sites, and stay for the evening light show.
items.why: Many people find it more beautiful than Chichén Itzá.
flow: Pyramid of the Magician, Nunnery Quadrangle, Governor's Palace.

items.name: Chichén Itzá
items.summary: The great Maya city with El Castillo and the largest ball court in Mesoamerica.
items.expect: Two hours each way; arrive at opening to beat the Cancún tours.
items.tip: Leave Mérida at 6 am, then swim at Cenote Ik Kil and stop in Valladolid.
items.why: One of the New Seven Wonders.

items.name: Cuzamá cenotes
items.summary: Three underground cenotes reached by horse-drawn rail cart along old henequen tracks.
items.expect: Ladders down into the caves; bring cash.
items.tip: Go on a weekday morning.
items.why: Unusually atmospheric swimming holes.
flow: Car or bus to Cuzamá, an hour.
Cart to each cenote and swim.

items.name: Celestún flamingos
items.summary: A biosphere reserve where boats take you through mangroves to flocks of pink flamingos.
items.expect: Ninety minutes each way; flamingo numbers peak from November to March.
items.tip: Share a boat at the bridge and have fish lunch on the beach.
items.why: The largest flamingo colony you can reach easily.

items.name: La Chaya Maya
items.summary: A colonial house where women make tortillas by hand as you watch, serving the Yucatecan classics.
items.expect: Queues at lunch; quick service.
items.tip: Order the sampler to try several dishes.
items.why: The easiest place to learn Yucatecan food.
flow: Sopa de lima, then cochinita pibil.

items.name: Mercado Lucas de Gálvez
items.summary: The main city market, with counters serving cochinita and seafood cocktails.
items.expect: Crowded, busy and best in the morning.
items.tip: Eat cochinita tacos at a counter for breakfast.
items.why: The real Mérida, at its cheapest.
flow: Browse, then eat at the counters upstairs.

items.name: Manjar Blanco
items.summary: A homey restaurant known for classic Yucatecan stews and desserts.
items.expect: Small and popular; lunch is the main meal.
items.tip: Try the relleno negro.
items.why: Home-style cooking locals return to.
flow: A stew, then the house dessert.

name: Oaxaca
cover: Santo Domingo de Guzmán Church, Oaxaca
summary: Mexico's food and craft capital: a colonial city of green stone churches, markets and seven moles, in a valley of mezcal villages and ancient Zapotec cities.
seasonNote: Day of the Dead (31 October to 2 November) and the Guelaguetza festival in late July are the busiest times; book months ahead.
arrival: Oaxaca airport is 20 minutes away; flights from Mexico City take an hour; ADO buses take about 6 hours.
gettingAround: Walk the centre; colectivos and tours run to Monte Albán, Hierve el Agua and the craft villages.
cashTip: Markets and colectivos are cash only.
foodTip: Mole negro, tlayudas, tamales in banana leaf, quesillo cheese, chapulines (grasshoppers) and mezcal.
buyTip: Black pottery from San Bartolo Coyotepec, alebrije carvings, rugs from Teotitlán del Valle and mezcal.
baseArea: The Centro, near Santo Domingo or Jalatlaco

connections.note: Frequent flights; ADO buses take 6 hours.

items.name: Templo de Santo Domingo and the Cultural Centre
items.wiki: Santo Domingo de Guzmán Church, Oaxaca
items.summary: A baroque church covered inside in gilded stucco, beside a former monastery museum and an ethnobotanical garden.
items.expect: The garden is by guided tour only, at set times.
items.tip: See the Mixtec gold of Tomb 7 in the museum.
items.why: The finest building in Oaxaca.
flow: Garden tour if the times fit.

items.name: Monte Albán
items.summary: The Zapotec capital on a levelled mountain top above the valley, with pyramids and a great plaza.
items.expect: Little shade; shuttles run from the centre.
items.tip: Go in the morning and climb the south platform for the view.
items.why: A UNESCO World Heritage site and one of Mesoamerica's first cities.
flow: Great Plaza, ball court, south platform.

items.name: Hierve el Agua
items.summary: Mineral springs that formed petrified waterfalls on a cliff, with pools at the edge.
items.expect: Two hours each way on mountain roads; occasionally closed by local disputes.
items.tip: Combine with Mitla, the Tule tree and a mezcal distillery on one day.
items.why: One of the strangest landscapes in Mexico.
flow: Swim in the pools, walk down to the falls.

items.name: Mitla
items.summary: A Zapotec religious centre with walls of intricate stone mosaics found nowhere else.
items.expect: A compact site in a village.
items.tip: Stop at the Árbol del Tule, one of the world's widest trees, on the way.
items.why: The most refined stone decoration in Mesoamerica.
flow: Hall of the Columns, then the mosaic patios.

items.name: Mezcal distillery tour
items.summary: A visit to a family palenque where agave hearts are roasted in earth pits and crushed by stone wheels.
items.expect: Tastings are generous; do not drive.
items.tip: Choose a small producer rather than a large brand visitor centre.
items.why: Oaxaca makes most of the world's mezcal.
flow: Tour or taxi to Santiago Matatlán.
Roasting pit, the stone mill, then a tasting.

items.name: Teotitlán del Valle
items.summary: A Zapotec weaving village where families dye wool with cochineal and indigo and weave rugs at home.
items.expect: Workshops welcome visitors; no pressure to buy.
items.tip: Ask to see the cochineal dye demonstration.
items.why: The best place to buy a rug directly from its maker.
flow: A family workshop, then the market and church.

items.name: Mercado 20 de Noviembre
items.summary: A market with a famous smoke-filled 'meat hall' where you choose meat and have it grilled on the spot.
items.expect: Smoky, noisy and fun; vendors call to you.
items.tip: Buy tasajo and chorizo in the Pasillo de Humo, then tortillas and salsas from the women at the end.
items.why: Oaxaca's most memorable meal.
flow: Two blocks south of the zócalo.
Choose meat, grab a table, add sides.

items.name: Los Danzantes
items.summary: A modern Oaxacan restaurant in an open-air courtyard, with its own mezcal.
items.expect: Smart casual; dinner fills up.
items.tip: Order a mole and the house mezcal flight.
items.why: A polished introduction to Oaxacan cooking.

items.name: Tlayudas Doña Martha
items.summary: An evening street grill making tlayudas, large crisp tortillas folded over beans, cheese and meat.
items.expect: Night only; plastic tables on the pavement.
items.tip: Order one to share and add tasajo.
items.why: Oaxaca's favourite late-night food.

name: San Miguel de Allende · Guanajuato
tagline: Pink church, cobbled streets and colonial silver towns
summary: A beautifully kept colonial town of ochre houses and a pink neo-Gothic church, popular with artists. The silver city of Guanajuato, built into a ravine, is an hour away.
seasonNote: At 1,900 metres, nights are cool from November to February; rain falls in summer afternoons. Holy Week and Day of the Dead are busy.
arrival: Fly to Querétaro or León (about 1 hour 15 minutes by shuttle) or take a 4-hour bus from Mexico City.
gettingAround: Walk; streets are cobbled and steep. Buses and shuttles link Guanajuato.
cashTip: Cards in restaurants; cash for markets and taxis.
foodTip: Enchiladas mineras in Guanajuato, rooftop dinners in San Miguel and churros at night.
buyTip: Tin and copper crafts, Talavera pottery and papier-mâché in the Mercado de Artesanías.
baseArea: The Centro, within walking distance of the Jardín

items.name: Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel
items.summary: A pink sandstone church whose neo-Gothic towers were designed by a self-taught local mason.
items.expect: Lit at night; mariachis on the Jardín in the evening.
items.tip: Come at dusk and sit in the Jardín opposite.
items.why: The symbol of San Miguel.
flow: Inside the church, then the Jardín.

items.name: Centro Histórico walk
items.summary: Cobbled streets of painted colonial houses, courtyards, galleries and churches.
items.expect: Steep in places; wear flat shoes.
items.tip: Walk up to the Mirador on Calle Salida a Querétaro for sunset.
items.why: A UNESCO World Heritage town.
flow: Calle Aldama, Bellas Artes, then the Mirador.

items.name: Fábrica La Aurora
items.summary: A former textile mill turned into galleries, studios and design shops.
items.expect: Some studios close on Sundays.
items.tip: Go late morning and have lunch at the café inside.
items.why: The centre of San Miguel's art scene.

items.name: El Charco del Ingenio
items.summary: A botanical garden of cacti and succulents around a canyon above the town.
items.expect: Rough paths; hot at midday.
items.tip: Go early or late afternoon for the views.
items.why: A peaceful escape with the best natural view of San Miguel.

items.name: Sanctuary of Atotonilco
items.summary: A country church whose every wall and ceiling is painted with folk-baroque murals.
items.expect: 15 minutes by taxi; a working pilgrimage site.
items.tip: Combine with a soak at La Gruta hot springs nearby.
items.why: Called the Sistine Chapel of Mexico.

items.name: Guanajuato
items.summary: A colourful silver-mining city stacked up a ravine, with roads in tunnels under the old town.
items.expect: An hour and a half by bus; hilly lanes and many students.
items.tip: Take the funicular to the Pípila viewpoint and join a callejoneada evening walking serenade.
items.why: A UNESCO World Heritage city and arguably Mexico's prettiest.
flow: Jardín de la Unión, Teatro Juárez, the funicular, the Callejón del Beso.

items.name: The Restaurant
items.summary: A courtyard restaurant of seasonal modern Mexican cooking by chef Donnie Masterton.
items.expect: Smart and popular; dinner fills up.
items.tip: Book a table in the courtyard.
items.why: San Miguel's most consistent fine dinner.
flow: Three courses from the seasonal menu.

items.name: Mercado Ignacio Ramírez
items.summary: The town food market, leading into the craft market, with cheap fondas serving lunch.
items.expect: Busy in the morning.
items.tip: Have gorditas at a fonda, then browse the crafts.
items.why: Local food at local prices.
flow: Lunch counter, then the Mercado de Artesanías.

items.name: San Agustín churrería
items.summary: A café famous for fresh churros and thick hot chocolate.
items.expect: A queue in the evening.
items.tip: Order the Mexican chocolate, not the Spanish one.
items.why: The town's favourite treat.
